semantic_correction.stem: During admission, a client asks what an advance directive is intended to do. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: It records healthcare wishes and/or names a representative for future medical treatment if the client later cannot make decisions.
options.B: It gives a representative authority to replace the client’s current healthcare choices as soon as the document is completed.
options.C: It converts healthcare preferences into medical orders that are implemented without a separate clinical decision-making process.
options.D: It designates a person to control insurance benefits and other financial decisions whenever future healthcare is required.

semantic_correction.rationale: Current CMS Advance Care Planning guidance describes an advance directive as a written document used to appoint a representative and/or record a person's wishes for future medical treatment in the event the person becomes incapacitated and unable to make decisions. Option A matches that purpose. Option B incorrectly states that completing the document necessarily replaces a capable client's current healthcare choices; activation and representative authority are governed by applicable law and document terms, and state law can differ. Option C confuses an advance directive with a medical order and overstates automatic implementation. Option D confuses a healthcare advance directive with authority over insurance or other financial decisions. Therefore A is the best answer.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Explain the core purpose of an advance directive as documenting future healthcare wishes and/or identifying a healthcare representative for circumstances in which the client cannot make decisions.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Medicare Coverage Database
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Revision effective November 1, 2023; current CMS Medicare Coverage Database page accessed 2026-08-19
semantic_correction.source_locator: Coverage Indications, Limitations, and/or Medical Necessity — definition of advance directive and decision-making capacity; CMS National Coverage Policy cites 42 CFR §§ 489.100 and 489.102
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: CMS describes an advance directive as a written document used to appoint a representative and/or record wishes for future medical treatment if the patient becomes incapacitated and unable to make decisions; capacity is assessed before deeming a patient unable to speak for themself.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: the original technical flag was an absolute-word distractor, but full legal re-audit identified a more important state-law precision problem: surrogate authority does not universally begin only after incapacity because activation rules and document terms vary. The item was rebuilt around the nationally supportable CMS definition/purpose of an advance directive, all choices were re-authored without absolute-word cueing, and the exact NCSBN Management of Care locator was verified.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original answer stated that the agent speaks when the client cannot do so, which was too universal for a national item because state statutes can permit immediately exercisable surrogate authority while preserving the capable principal's controlling wishes. The construct was narrowed to the CMS-supported purpose of an advance directive rather than making a universal activation-rule claim.
audit_findings_append.source_locator: Advance Care Planning L38970 — advance-directive definition and capacity discussion
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Management of Care, printed p. 7 / PDF p. 11 — Integrate advance directives into client plan of care

option_audit.A: Correct. It matches the CMS description of an advance directive as documenting future healthcare wishes and/or appointing a representative for circumstances in which the person cannot make decisions.
option_audit.B: Plausible confusion about healthcare-agent authority, but it incorrectly says completion itself replaces the capable client's current choices; authority timing is law/document dependent and this is not the CMS definition of the directive's purpose.
option_audit.C: Plausible confusion with portable medical orders, but an advance directive does not by itself convert all preferences into automatically implemented treatment orders without clinical decision-making.
option_audit.D: Plausible confusion with a financial power of attorney, but the cited healthcare advance-directive construct concerns future medical-treatment wishes and/or healthcare representation, not control of insurance or general finances.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A alone states the CMS-defined healthcare purpose without making a state-specific activation claim; B, C, and D each conflate the document with a different legal or clinical function.

cueing_check.note: All four options are parallel descriptions of document purpose/function and are naturally similar in length; no mechanical padding was added.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: Explaining and integrating advance directives and protecting client rights are explicit Management of Care activities for the newly licensed RN.
